# Work

> Work is a free, open-source desktop app for getting work done with AI agents: your projects, a real browser, terminals and editors, and agents that reshape the app and build tools for you. It runs on your Mac, uses the AI accounts you already pay for, and keeps your work on your machine unless you choose to run your own server.

> Canonical copy: https://work.software/llms.txt (this file mirrors it with repository-relative links; keep both in step, see docs in the website repository).

Work is the product; Catamorphic is the open-source framework it is built on. Both live in one repository: https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic (Apache-2.0).

## Facts

- Product: Work, "the software for work"
- Framework underneath: Catamorphic (same repository)
- License: Apache-2.0
- Price: free; no account, subscription or hosted service required
- Platform: macOS 12 or newer on Apple silicon (desktop); a mobile web companion; the Work server, a self-hosted Docker image
- Install: `brew install --cask opencx-labs/tap/work@alpha`, or the DMG on https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic/releases
- AI: your own Claude Code or Codex account, or API keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter); providers bill you directly
- Data: stays on your Mac by default; optionally on a server you run
- Work server: `ghcr.io/opencx-labs/work-server`, published with every release (tags: the release version, `alpha`, and `latest` for Stable); one `docker run` with zero external services, `DATABASE_URL` opts into Postgres
- Connect other tools: MCP (a project on your server is an MCP endpoint)
- Website: https://work.software
- This guide, with the linked documents inlined: https://work.software/llms-full.txt
- Source of truth for capabilities: the repository's README and decision records (links below)

## What matters most

- **Open source and free, no strings attached.** Apache-2.0 license. No account, no subscription, no hosted service required. Nothing leaves your machine unless you send it.
- **It is a browser.** Work embeds a real Chromium browser: tabs, Chrome-style profiles, bookmarks (pinned tiles and lists, per project too), history, and a password manager: it offers to save sign-ins, suggests saved logins under the field, generates strong passwords for new accounts, and keeps notes with each login, unlocked with Touch ID. It keeps passkeys too: sites can create them, you sign in with Touch ID from a sheet or the field suggestions, and passkeys and passwords import from Bitwarden or KeePassXC (passwords from a CSV file too). Security keys work alongside. Tabs you have not looked at for a while sleep to free memory and reopen where you left off, as in Chrome. Agents drive it as you would, in your signed-in tabs: real clicks and typing, uploads and downloads, and a page's console, network and JavaScript for web development. You can use it as a clean browser and nothing more.
- **It uses your existing AI subscriptions.** Sign in with the Claude Code or Codex account you already have, or add API keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter). Providers charge you directly; Work adds nothing.
- **Completely local, or your own server.** The desktop app runs with an embedded database and local sandboxes; no cloud. When you want your work and agents available from your phone or while the Mac sleeps, run the Work server yourself (one Docker container published with every release, `apps/server`) and keep everything on hardware you control. A company brain on that server can admit only its Google Workspace accounts, revokes a departed person's access within minutes, gives agents reviewed access to company systems without handing them credentials, and shares specific documents, folders, or apps with customers behind their own sign-in.
- **Completely customizable.** The sidebars and command palette modes, theme, shortcuts, tabs, notifications and terminal macros are plain files (`workspace.js`, `theme.json`, settings). Ask the assistant to change them and it edits the files; the app updates live. Agents build apps and workflows inside a project that look and behave like built-in parts of the app.
- **Three ways to use it.** A coding workspace (worktrees, terminals, editors, diffs, pull requests, several coding harnesses side by side). A company brain (shared projects, roles and memberships, automations, apps, tuned agent roles, reachable from desktop, mobile PWA or any MCP client). Or just a nice, clean browser with an assistant a keystroke away.

## Why it exists

We built Work because we believe one well-built piece of software can replace most productivity and collaboration tools. Software is now cheap; as humans, we just need to find the optimal form for it, make it open source, and let it build itself afterwards.

## How it works

- A project is an ordinary folder and a git repository. Every agent turn that changes files becomes a checkpoint commit; you can inspect diffs or trust routine work to continue.
- Chats float over whatever you are doing (a page, a document, a terminal) and can be minimized to a dock. Agents see the workspace context you give them: the page, the file, the terminal.
- Agents can be Claude Code, Codex, or API models (multi-harness), with per-agent permission mode (each harness's own, such as Claude Code's plan, auto or bypass permissions, or Codex's sandbox and approvals), sandboxing, memory, skills, instructions and effort. Connectors (MCP) attach to profiles and agents.
- Every chat is a durable log of turns, the same on the desktop, the phone and the server, streamed live. Questions and approvals can be answered from any of them, a message sent while an agent waits on a question reaches it in the same turn, a turn whose machine stopped is picked up by another and continues on the agent's own conversation, and any turn can be undone with the files it changed.
- Agents write durable workflows (TypeScript, run in sandboxes, resumable) and apps (small React screens built from Work's component kit). An app can read your own chats in a project after you allow it once; it never sees anyone else's.
- Automations run for you or for the whole project. A workflow starts from a schedule, a chat event, or a webhook sent to your server (GitHub's included; on the desktop, GitHub is polled into the same events), and can message your chat or a shared project chat that anyone in the project can continue (one per pull request review, one per inbound request). On a Work server, people joining, leaving, or changing groups in the company directory start workflows too, so a new engineer's keys are issued as they join and revoked as they leave. Projects define their own triggers, such as "a pull request was merged" or "someone mentioned the app in Slack", on top of webhooks, with filters that decide which events start a run; webhooks check each sender's signature scheme and answer its setup handshake.
- Slack is built the same way, from project code rather than a built-in integration: mentioning the app in a Slack thread starts or continues a shared project chat for that thread, the agent reads the thread (and, given a search token, searches Slack) through the gateway, which holds the tokens, and its answer is posted back to the thread. Slack's retries of an event start no second run.
- Pull request review is built the same way: every pull request in a connected repository gets a code and security review in its own shared chat on a dedicated review pool. The reviewer checks out the pull request's head, installs, builds, and runs the tests and the change's services in its own sandbox, checks migrations against a read-only production replica, and posts a review with inline comments and a check run; each push moves the same chat to the new head, mentions in comments are answered on the pull request, and merging or closing it releases everything the review held. The whole automation is plain files in the project that the team can edit.
- Agents run long commands in the background, on the desktop and on the Work server, where they run inside the agent's own workspace and stop when the chat closes. On the desktop agents can also watch a command (a deploy, a file, a status page); the chat wakes when it finishes, succeeds or changes, including after the computer sleeps.
- The mobile companion (a PWA) pairs with the desktop by QR code over your LAN, or connects to your server, so a chat can continue from your phone.
- The Work server is a company brain in one image. People sign in through Google Workspace: only the company domain gets in, people suspended or removed in the directory are signed out within minutes, and directory groups can map to project roles. Agents and workflows reach MCP servers, HTTP APIs and a production database through a gateway that holds the keys; database access is read-only with cost and row limits, and a company can add its own guards in code (a model reviewer, a person's approval, or both) to review each action. Organization administrators connect each system once, from the app or the server, and projects choose which of those connections each environment may use in a reviewed project file. Project secrets are sealed in an encrypted vault. Enrolled workers add execution capacity holding only a machine credential, never the database or secrets; each worker serves everyone, named people and groups, or one project's own automations and shared chats, so a person's agents run on their own machine first, and machine rules can give every member of a directory group a machine of their own: a Hetzner Cloud server created for them, or one of the company's own servers enrolled into a pool, each set up by the same install script. A departed person's machine stops taking work at once and is kept for a set number of days, then destroyed or wiped and returned to its pool. Agents use Git in their sandboxes the ordinary way: fetches and pushes go through the gateway with a short-lived session grant, never the remote's credential, pushes are limited to the project's work branches, and automations can start a chat's checkout at any ref of the project's remote, such as a pull request's head, and move it when the pull request changes. Project agents can be Claude Code or Codex on the server too: the CLI runs in the chat's sandbox, on a worker or the server, and reaches its model through the gateway, which holds the organization's model key, allows only the models the environment names, and records usage per chat. Developers can instead use their own Claude Code and Codex subscriptions in their own remote chats on machines where they signed in themselves, such as a worker at home: Work never copies or forwards a sign-in, and a chat on a subscription runs only on a machine holding that person's sign-in. Files such as `.env` that are never committed can travel with them; they reach only that person's chats, in environments that allow it, on machines that isolate that person. A chat started on their own computer moves to a server environment and continues there with its history. A single machine stays one `docker run`.
- On the Work server each project Environment chooses the image its agents run in (a registry image or a Dockerfile reviewed in the project), whether they get their own Docker and Docker Compose, and which hosts they may reach. An agent's sandboxing is enforced by the server: a contained reviewer can run anything in its sandbox but changes nothing outside it and only reads through connections, a propose agent proposes but does not publish, and a publish agent may deploy and publish. Sandboxing is separate from the harness's own permission mode, which each agent also chooses. When an unattended agent needs approval, the people its automation named get a notification and answer from their own chats.
- Shares send customers or partners a sign-in link to one document, folder or live app. They sign in with their own account (for example your product's own sign-in over OpenID Connect) and see only what was shared.
- A company adds its own code (guards, directories, connection providers, routes) by extending the image with `@catamorphic/work-server` hooks instead of forking. Anyone can ask their coding agent to set up a Work server with the setup skill, and members work from Claude Code or any MCP client connected to the project's MCP endpoint with their own roles: read and search the project, draft, check and deploy workflows and apps, run workflows and read their runs, ask the project's agents, and share with customers.
- Privacy: incognito chats stay on the device and are never mirrored; a project's private working files are separate from shared project source.

## Install

- Mac with Apple silicon, macOS 12 or newer. Preview channel: `brew install --cask opencx-labs/tap/work@alpha`, or download the signed DMG from https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic/releases.
- Downloads and release notes: https://github.com/opencx-labs/catamorphic/releases
